Coding academies are fantastic for those with an older CS degree who wish to break into a new language as quickly as possible. For normal 9 to 5 workers looking for a new career these academies are probably a poor choice compared to normal courses from an established local university or local community college. LOL at anyone who thinks programming will be eliminated by visual building environments. I remember hearing that same line when WYSIWYG editors came out for building HTML pages.

Having been a web developer for a few years I think that one truth has stood out to me: all prophecies about how programming is evolving and how so much of what we use now will be obsolete fail to take into account one thing; large organizations adopt at a glacial pace.

Even proven bad practices remain because they are so deeply ingrained in the work flow. The sheer amount of technical debt accumulated seems to be acceptable so long as the site/application stays up and brings in money. Job openings may decline, but some will remain.

I didn't read the article because I'm not entirely sure I would hear anything new, so I won't comment on it specifically. I don't think coding academies are nonsense, but I'm not sure how effective they are because of their reception by employers. Some people need a school-like structure. They to be dictated to about mental exercises that produce something that may or may not be reusable later on. Other people can't stand it but thrive on figuring it out on their own in their own way.

I see them, conceptually, as a good thing. If someone wants to learn how to do Ruby on Rails (as an example), I really don't think they need a biology, operating system theory, and health classes. Even more wasteful is to teach programming in one language if the person wants to use another in the end.

That said, rushing someone through things in 3 months makes them a junior at best and a paid intern at worst. If any code school gives any other impression then they're being deceptive.
